titre: The Forest That Communicates, and the Missing Evidence
accroche: Trees are said to exchange resources and signals through an underground network. Three biologists checked the evidence
contenu_vulgarise:
The idea has been everywhere for about ten years, under the name *wood wide web*. The trees of a forest are said to be linked by a network of fungal filaments; they supposedly trade carbon, water and nutrients through it; mother trees would feed their offspring and send out warning signals when a pest attacks.

It has fed bestselling books, documentaries, a complete rethinking of how we look at the forest.

In 2023, three biologists set out to go back over the scientific publications cited in support of these claims.

## What Is Established

Part of the case is solid, and that is where to begin.

Mycorrhizae exist: they are associations between a plant's roots and a fungus, in which each supplies what the other cannot produce. The fungus provides the plant with water and minerals that it gathers over an immense surface; the plant provides it with sugars from photosynthesis. It is one of the most widespread symbioses in the living world.

That a single fungus can connect to the roots of several trees at once is also documented. And transfers of carbon from one plant to another by this route have indeed been measured, in the laboratory or under controlled conditions.

## What the Check Found

The article published in *Nature Ecology & Evolution* examines three claims and concludes, for each, that the literature does not establish what it is made to say.

That these networks are widespread in forests has not been demonstrated: field studies are few, and their results vary too much to generalize.

That the transfers improve the growth of seedlings is no better established: the measured effects go both ways, and other explanations, the fungus is simply offloading its surplus, the roots are touching, have not been ruled out.

That adult trees preferentially feed their own offspring or send them defense signals: for this claim, the authors find no peer-reviewed publication at all.

The authors also point to a citation bias. Work favorable to the network is cited far more often than null or negative results, so that the literature looks, from a distance, more conclusive than it is.

## What the Case Shows

None of the three authors claims that the network does not exist. They say that we do not know, and that public discourse has gotten well ahead of what we do know.

The mechanism deserves attention because it assumes no dishonesty. An appealing hypothesis attracts work that tests it; the studies that confirm it are cited, published, taken up; those that find nothing stay in a drawer. After twenty years, an entire literature leans, without any single study being false.

repere.texte: The claim that adult trees preferentially send resources and defense signals to their offspring through the mycorrhizal network rests on no peer-reviewed publication.
repere.source: Karst, Jones & Hoeksema, “Positive citation bias and overinterpreted results lead to misinformation on common mycorrhizal networks in forests,” Nature Ecology & Evolution, 7, 2023

carte.punch: No study is false. The entire literature leans anyway.
carte.idee: Trees are said to exchange resources and alerts through a fungal network. Going back over the cited publications, three biologists find that work favorable to the idea is cited far more than null results.
carte.source_courte: Karst et al., Nat. Ecol. Evol., 2023

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Karst, Jones & Hoeksema (2023), Nature Ecology & Evolution
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: In English; the three claims are treated separately, each in a few pages.

quiz.question: What do the authors fault in the literature on mycorrhizal networks?
choix: For publishing fabricated results to support an appealing hypothesis
For citing favorable results far more readily than null results
For confusing mycorrhizae with another type of root symbiosis
For relying solely on field observations, without experimentation
quiz.explication: No fraud is at issue, and the existence of mycorrhizae is not disputed. The bias is bibliographic: work confirming the hypothesis is taken up, while work that finds nothing stays little cited, so the literature looks more conclusive than it is. Field studies are in fact what is most lacking.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the three biologists say about carbon transfers measured between plants via the mycorrhizal route?
choix: That they have never been observed, even in the laboratory
That they have indeed been measured in the laboratory or under controlled conditions
That they concern only genetically close tree species
That they are due to a methodological error in every published study
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card specifies that carbon transfers between plants by this route have indeed been measured in the laboratory or under controlled conditions: this point is part of what is established.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the authors say about the claim that adult trees preferentially feed their own offspring?
choix: That it is confirmed by several independent field studies
That it concerns only certain conifer species, not broadleaf trees
That they found no peer-reviewed publication that establishes it
That it was explicitly refuted by a study published in 2023
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On this specific point, the authors find no peer-reviewed publication that establishes it, which makes it the least supported of the three claims examined.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Regarding the idea that mycorrhizal networks are widespread in forests, what do the authors find?
choix: That field studies are few and their results too variable to generalize
That no field study has ever been conducted on this question
That the question has been definitively settled by scientific consensus in their favor
That only tropical forests have this type of network
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The authors note that field studies on this subject are few and that their results vary too much to allow generalizing to forests as a whole.
